subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

speechtext:
-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider a proposed resolution to repeal the Dominion Housing Act, 1935, and reenact certain provisions thereof with amendments and additions thereto; and to make certain provisions with respect to low rental houses and municipal taxes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is preliminary to the introduction of a national housing act. The new act will be divided into three parts, each distinct and whole in itself and attempting to deal with a specific phase of the housing problem.
Part I involves the repeal of the Dominion Housing Act and the reenactment of parts of it, together with important changes and additions designed to bring the facilities of this act to individuals and communities that have not hitherto benefited from it. This part of the legislation, part I, is intended solely for families who wish to own their own homes, and strong emphasis is placed upon facilities for families in the lower income brackets and in the small and remote communities.
Part II contemplates an experiment on a comprehensive scale in the low rental housing field, about which we have heard so much in this house and in the country in the last few years.
Part III is intended as an attack on the major obstacle retarding the building of new houses, the high level of real property taxes.
It is unnecessary for me, I am sure, at this stage to spend any time in dealing with the social and economic evils of insanitary, unsafe or inadequate housing accommodation or with the advantages to our people and our economy of raising the standard of housing conditions and restoring a more normal level of activity in the great group of construction and building supply industries which play so important a part in sustaining employment in normal times, which suffered perhaps more than any other industry from the effects of the depression, and which have been the most laggard of our industries in recovering from the depression. All these considerations are well known to the house. I' can assume, therefore, that there will be a keen and sympathetic appreciation of the objectives
National Housing Act

which this legislation seeks, which I would define as (1) a substantial contribution to the elimination of unemployment in a field where it has been most heavily concentrated, and to the general stimulation of business recovery; and (2) a substantial contribution to the improvement of housing conditions, particularly for families of low income, at the same time giving our people, our provincial and municipal governments and the house building industry, a lead as to sound methods and policies that may be followed in the future.
While a real effort has been made to get substantial results and to get them promptly, I think a careful examination of the legislation which will follow this resolution will also indicate that care has been taken to safeguard the interests of the dominion and to surround the various parts of the program with provisions to ensure safe and sound businesslike procedure.
I said a few moments ago that part I repeals and reenacts part of the present Dominion Housing Act, with important changes and additions. It will be remembered that the present Dominion Housing Act was passed in 1935. It followed an examination by a committee of the house of the housing question and was the subject of extended debate in this house before it became law. Very little was done; in fact I do not think any loans were made under the Dominion Housing Act of 1935 by the former government. The act was there when the present government came into office, and we have been operating under its provisions ever since.
It early became apparent, however, that there were certain grave defects in the operation of the present Dominion Housing Act. The government endeavoured to meet those defects in so far as the powers contained in the act would permit the government to do so. We did, in fact, in September, 1936, by the changed regulations then put into effect liberalize the operation of the act very materially. However, I think it will be recognized by all who have followed the operation of the Dominion Housing Act that it suffers from at least two grave deficiencies; but before saying that I should at any rate give the Dominion Housing Act this commendation : It was the first effort in this country to deal with the problem of housing by the dominion- parliament; and in spite of the defects and the weaknesses which have developed in operation, it should be noted that prior to May 31 of this year, 4,249 family

housing units have been financed under this act, involving an aggregate expenditure of $17,350,000, and as of that date the average loan per family unit was $4,083.
As a consequence of the broadened regulations made available in September, 1936, there has been a considerable acceleration of lending activity under the act, but it nevertheless remains true that the total volume of this lending activity has been substantially less than is desirable. Moreover, the defects to which I have previously referred are as follows: First, the unwillingness of the lending institutions to make loans in many small and remote communities, and second, the reluctance of the lending institutions to make loans for small amounts in what they regard as the less desirable residential areas of the larger urban communities, despite the fact that these districts are, in many instances, the only areas in which it is possible for the people in the relatively low income groups to build houses for themselves.
Those are the main defects of the original legislation, and part I of the new bill seeks to remedy them. The new provisions of part I, I shall now endeavour to summarize briefly, but naturally I shall have to await the production of the detailed bill, which is necessarily somewhat complex, before entering into a general debate on the matter.
In the normal case of a loan under part I- and I use the word " normal " as distinct from the special low cost provisions to which I shall later refer-a housing loan may in future be made for from 70 to 80 per cent of the lending value of the new house, and of this total, whatever it may be, the dominion will advance 25 per cent, and the private lending institution or local municipal authority, as the case may be, 75 per cent. Under the old legislation the dominion's advance was 20 per cent of the lending value, and the maximum amount of the joint loan was 80 per cent, with provision made by regulation for 75 per cent and 80 per cent loans in certain cases as well. This change will simplify accounting, lessen bookkeeping costs, and eliminate the temptation to manipulate estimates of cost and of appraised value in order to bring the loan within the existing 70, 75 or 80 per cent categories. Provision will be made in the bill that in the case where the lending value does not exceed $2,500- that is the definitely low cost house-a loan may be made up to 90 per cent, of which the dominion is to advance its 25 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Yes. I wish my hon. friends would be good enough to defer their detailed questions. I must admit this matter is quite complex, and I am desirous of making a detailed statement, after which I shall be glad to deal with questions.
I have just stated that one of the new provisions involves the possibility of a 90 per cent loan by the lending institution, in the case where the lending value is $2,500 or less, and of this 90 per cent loan the dominion will advance its 25 per cent. That is to take care of the case where it is difficult for the individual to put up a minimum equity of 20 per cent at the start. Under Canadian conditions, with the risks of change in property values and changing conditions of employment, I do not claim that 90 per cent loans give a sufficient margin of protection to the lender; nor am I sure that it is normally a kindness to the individual to encourage him to attempt the risk of home ownership with only a 10 per cent equity. Nevertheless I know there are in this country thousands of individuals in the lowest income groups who pay a large percentage of their total income for the rent of necessary housing accommodation, and consequently it is very difficult for them to put aside each month the small amount in savings that might be expected to give them, over a period of years, a 20 per cent equity in a home. The government is prepared, therefore, to try as an experiment 90 per cent loans in cases where the lending value of the property does not exceed $2,500. If an individual wishes to build a home at a higher cost than this. I think we are justified in requiring him first to build up a 20 per cent equity in the form of either a lot, or cash, or both. It will be clear, of course, that to justify lending institutions in making this type of loan, it will be necessary to give them a more effective inducement, of which I shall now speak.
I am confident, I may say, that we shall be able to get the consent of at least some lending institutions to make these small high percentage loans to deserving people in certain sections of our larger cities, in the suburban and rural areas, in fishing villages, mining towns, and small urban communities generally.
The most important change which we are proposing in this part of the bill to deal with, the matter to which I have just been referring, involves the application of the home improvement plan principle of a pooled guarantee, in respect of loans made by lending institutions and falling into certain definite categories. It will be observed that the home improvement act, which was put on the statutes a year ago, and under which some $17,000,000 have now been advanced for home improvements, involves the pooled principle; that is to say, the government's guarantee of 15 per cent under the home improvement act applies to the aggregate losses of the lending institution operating under the law.
As regards the experience up to date-it is a little early to speak of final results, though I can assure the house that the losses are running substantially below the amount of the guarantee-it is such as to warrant the government in attempting to apply the same principle with respect to the construction of low cost houses. In other words, we are asking for authority to enter into contracts with lendiug institutions under which we will guarantee them against loss up to a maximum of 20 per cent of the total amount of 80 per cent loans made by them which do not exceed $4,000 each for a single family dwelling, and made in such communities or districts as may be designated by the minister, and up to a maximum of 25 per cent guarantee in the case of 90 per cent loans. I hope I have made that clear. The application of the pooled guarantee principle is for the purpose of inducing and justifying the lenders in making loans in communities remote from the larger centres, small communities which as an ordinary business proposition do not commend themselves to lending institutions, both because of the cost of looking after a few loans involving considerable travelling expenses, and also because of the security factor involved in the low re-sale value of property situate where sales are infrequent, as is the case in rural communities as compared with our'larger urban centres. So we say, to express that in another way, on all loans made in these areas, which must be defined by agreement, of $4,000 by a lending institution, a percentage guarantee against loss will be given to the lending institution, and the smaller the total amount of the loan and the larger the percentage which it bears to the lending value of the property, the higher will be the percentage of guarantee which the government will give as an inducement toward the financing of low-cost homes for owners thereof.
The figures I have just given, up to 25 per cent in the case of 90 per cent loans, are of course maximum figures. It is proposed not only to designate special areas, consisting of small and remote communities in which loans
National Housing Act

are not now being made, but also to develop a schedule of the amounts that the government guarantees, which will be graduated downwards in accordance with the size of the loan, say from three to four thousand dollars, and graduated upward in accordance with the percentage which the loan bears to the lending value, that is to say from 70 to 80 or 90 per cent. In other words, we may go up to the maximum of 20 per cent guarantee in the case of 80 per cent loans for $3,000 or less, but the guarantee which we will give with respect to a 70 per cent loan for an amount of $4,000 will be very much less, possibly, I should say offhand, 5 per cent. The development of a schedule of this sort is, of course, a difficult and complex process and cannot be fully detailed, I am afraid, in a statute.
A further important change in connection with part I is to make it possible for a payment to be made to a lending institution to assist it in defraying the special costs incurred in arranging loans, making appraisals, inspections and so forth in small and remote communities designated. This payment is not to exceed $20 for any one loan, plus a mileage allowance fixed by the minister for necessary travelling expenses based upon the distance from the nearest place from which the loan can be arranged and supervised by the lending institution. I am sure that members from many constituencies who have communicated with me from time to time about housing matters will appreciate the kind of difficulty which this amendment seeks to meet. I have had many communications from districts away from the larger centres complaining that no loans have been made in those communities. It is perfectly obvious that no lending institution can afford under present conditions to have its representatives make to such areas the several trips which are required in order to make a loan and inspect the house during the progress of construction. Nevertheless, residents of such communities naturally feel that they have as much right as residents of large urban areas to participate in the benefits of a national housing act. It will be necessary to designate the communities and areas in connection with which such assistance is to be given and to arrange for a schedule of allowances which will be payable in communities at varying distances from the nearest point from which the loan can be arranged by the lending institution.
Another new provision in part I increases the maximum amount which may be paid out by the minister in respect of advances, losses and expenses. A maximum of ten million dollars was the authority under the old act;

it is proposed to increase this authority to twenty million dollars. Under the old act the dominion has already committed itself to $4,500,000 in respect of the $17,300,000 housing construction to which I referred earlier. The figure of $20,000,000 provided in the resolution now before the house gives us under the authority a leeway of about $15,500,000 which, together with the funds advanced by the lending institutions under the provisions of the act, should make it possible to make aggregate loans up to $60,000,000 or more under this part of the national housing act.
There are other minor amendments in connection with part I which I think can be very much better taken up on the bill itself in committee, but I have endeavoured to outline the broad provisions effecting the changes. Part I, as I said at the outset, is designed for people who desire to own their own homes and it is designed to make it easier for them to do so. It is designed to make it easier for lending institutions to make loans to enable people to own their own homes, and every provision which has been changed has been designed, to use the term I used before, to "liberalize" the application of the act. I did not use the word political!}' in any sense. The other day when I used the word "conservatively" some of my hon. friends opposite were welcoming a new recruit, but I did not use that word politically either.
With respect to part II, this is designed to make possible a comprehensive experiment in the field of low rental housing. It is based upon acceptance of the arguments advanced in this connection by the national employment commission, and it follows in general though not in detail the main lines of the program suggested by that commission. In this connection I wish to stress a point made in the preamble to the bill. The preamble will point out that in some areas the housing conditions fall short of minimum standards of health and decency, and that these conditions may affect not only public health and morals, but the employability and efficiency of our working population. While the primary responsibility for decent, safe and sanitary housing conditions must rest, under our constitution, upon the province and upon the municipalities, nevertheless, the proposed dominion program is justified by emergency conditions, because it is designed to create needed employment, to direct attention to the importance of the housing problem generally, and to provide a basis of experience upon which the provinces and the municipalities may follow sound and proven policies in the future.

National Housing Act
Briefly, part II, low rental housing, provides that the minister, with the approval of the governor in council, may make loans to local housing authorities to assist in the construction of houses to be leased to families of low income. The aggregate principal amount of the loans under this part is not to exceed 830,000,000.
What are local housing authorities under the bill? Local housing authorities may consist of either of two types, depending upon whether on the one hand the municipality desires to enlist the cooperation of private enterprise in working out its low rental housing scheme, or whether on the other it desires to operate it entirely under the municipal authority. If the municipality desires to enlist the cooperation of private enterprise, private capital and business management of a private nature, it may do so through the medium of a limited dividend housing corporation with capital sufficient to provide for 20 per cent of the cost of the project. This capital, it is presumed, will be subscribed by public-spirited citizens who may be expected to plan, construct and administer the enterprise on sound business lines. They are limited in dividend on the capital they invest to a rate of 5 per cent, and from information I have it will be possible to organize such limited dividend housing corporations in some instances at a lower dividend maximum than this. Secondly, if the municipality desires to operate a low rental housing project under municipal auspices, it may do so through the medium of a commission or other body having authority to construct, hold and manage houses built as a low rental housing project, and in the case of a municipality doing the job itself in this manner it is required to put up an equity of only 10 per cent. In the case of a limited dividend housing corporation a 20 per cent equity will be required. In the case of a municipal housing corporation a 10 per cent equity will be required.
What will be the dominion's contribution? The dominion's contribution, which I think all will agree is substantial, is to be made on the basis of the dominion supplying the bulk of the funds, 80 per cent in the case of a limited dividend housing corporation and 90 per cent in the case of a municipality, at very low interest rates. In the case of a limited dividend housing corporation, where the equity subscribed privately must be at least 20 per cent, the interest rate will be If per cent per annum; and in the case of other local housing authorities, that is municipal bodies, where the equity required is only 10 per cent, the interest rate is two per cent per annum. Semi-annual payments must be made by the 51953-232
local housing authority to cover interest and to amortize the principal over a long period. In the case of a limited dividend housing corporation the semi-annual payment therefore will be seven-eighths of one per cent for interest and one per cent for amortization. In the case of a municipal local housing authority the semi-annual payment will be two per cent, of which one per cent represents interest and the remaining one per cent amortization. These rates of amortization in both cases will mean that the loans will be completely retired in between thirty-four and thirty-five years. That then is the dominion's contribution.
Let us now consider the provincial contribution. If the local housing authority is a municipal body, then under the same principle which was enunciated in connection with the municipal improvements assistance bill we must ask the provincial government to guarantee repayment of the amounts advanced by the dominion. As I stated on a former occasion, the municipalities are completely creatures of the provincial legislature. Changes made in municipal law by provincial legislatures may have the effect of rendering the security held by the dominion in connection with the project completely useless, and for that reason we believe we are justified, where the dominion is putting up 90 per cent of the amount to be invested in a low rental housing project operated by the municipality, in asking that the province should guarantee repayment to the dominion government of its loans in that regard. No such guarantee is asked of the provinces in connection with a scheme operated by a limited dividend housing corporation. Obviously the larger equity, double the amount, renders that less desirable, and from my point of view at least it has this advantage, that those municipalities which desire to undertake low rental housing projects will, I believe, be able to get going with the matter very much more quickly if they can interest public-spirited citizens in putting up 20 per cent of the cost through the medium of a limited dividend housing corporation than they will be able to do, by reason of delay due to changes in law which might be required in some cases before the municipal law would be sufficiently broad to enable them to operate municipally.
What must the municipality do? The municipality must have approved the project, and must have secured the guarantee from the province, if it is to be operated as a purely municipal project. The municipality must also agree that municipal taxes on the low

National Housing Act

rental housing project, during the period of its operation under this legislation, while there is any money owing to the dominion, shall not exceed one per cent annually of the cost of the whole project. We ask the municipality also in the case of the limited dividend corporation, in case they prefer this method, to agree that if the administration by that method involves a shortage in the amount due the dominion government, the municipality will reduce taxes still further to enable that amount to be made up. Not having the guarantee of the provincial government, we must there insist upon the closeness of municipal interest in the scheme and a degree of responsibility. The municipality must also agree not to levy taxes on the income of a local housing authority. Also, if the municipality is operating directly a low rental housing scheme, it must put up, as I said before, 10 per cent of the total cost, which of course may be and in most instances will take the form of land for the project. In addition, the municipality may-there is no "must" about this-make	additional
voluntary contributions to a rent reduction fund, which I shall describe a little later.
What about the rental provisions? No family housing unit in a low rental housing project is to be rented to a family whose family income is equal to more than five times the economic rental of the unit, unless there is no demand for the unit from families of lower income. The logic behind this provision is that a family can afford to pay about 20 per cent of its annual income for rent. If this 20 per cent is sufficient to pay the economic rental of housing accommodation, private enterprise should be able to provide sufficient housing accommodation without any special subsidy from the state. "Economic rental" is defined in the bill as a rental which gives a return of 9j per cent on the cost of construction plus the annual municipal taxes. Families of low income are defined as families whose total family income is less than five times the economic rental of a family housing unit built as part of the low rental housing project. The annual rental to be charged a family of low income is to be not in excess of 20 per cent of the total income of such family. Provision is also made for the possible establishment of a rent reduction fund by voluntary contributions from the province or the municipality concerned. These contributions are not compulsory; but if it is desired by the municipality to lease the accommodation at lower rates than are made possible by the annual carrying charge of the project, that is at rates low enough to meet the needs of families in the very lowest income group, then

the municipality and the province are in a position to reach this objective by making voluntary contributions to the rent reduction fund.
As far as safeguards are concerned, there will be provision that evidence of the need for a low rental housing project must be shown by the municipality concerned. The area must be adequately planned and zoned. The project must be of sufficient size to give reasonable economies. Economic design and sound construction will be required. The management of the local housing authority must be satisfactory. The terms of acquisition of the land must be satisfactory. The terms of the charter of any local housing authority must be satisfactory. The local housing authority must agree to keep the houses in a satisfactory state of repair, and keep books and accounts and make an annual report to the minister. A limited dividend housing corporation must give an option to the municipality to buy the project for the amount of the corporation's paid-up capital and any unpaid dividends. Let me repeat that in another form: If any municipality adopts the limited dividend housing corporation method of dealing with this problem, then the corporation, when formed, must give an option to the municipality enabling the municipality to take over the enterprise at any time, the amount to be paid being fixed by the amount of the paid-up capital of the corporation plus any accrued dividends. Thus those investing their money in low rental housing projects under the limited dividend corporation method are assured that they can at no time get more than 5 per cent return on their money, neither can they hope for any accretion in the capital value of their investment. A further provision is that if there is a breach of contract to pay, the amount of the loan may be declared due and payable or the interest rate may be increased.
Let us now consider the amount of loan which may be made in a municipality for the purpose of low rental housing projects. The total of the loans made in any municipality must not exceed that proportion of $30,000,000 which the population of the municipality bears to the total urban population of Canada on the basis of the 1931 census. That proportion, Mr. Speaker, will give ample opportunity for the development of large scale experiments, particularly in our larger centres, in the direction of low rental housing projects.
There may be some criticism at first sight because of the slightly lower rate of interest which it is proposed to charge a limited dividend housing corporation as compared with a municipality operating directly. After all,

National Housing Act
the private persons who organize a limited dividend housing corporation must put up an equity of twenty per cent, which is twice the amount of the equity required in the case of a municipal corporation. The private persons who organize such a corporation will be required to do a vast amount of work in connection with planning the project, supervising construction and managing the project during its useful life. Their dividends are limited to a maximum of five per cent, which is not a very high rate for individuals who are willing to risk a substantial amount of capital for thirty-four or thirty-five years. Then, of course, I have already referred to the other provision which ensures that the limited dividend housing corporation must give an option to the municipality which will preserve the right of the municipality to take over the project at the amount of the capital invested by the limited dividend corporation. Also I believe it desirable to give every inducement to get private capital to cooperate [DOT] in this task of solving the problem of families with low incomes, on a non-profit basis. I am sure not all but many municipalities would very much prefer to have limited dividend corporations of this sort take up the burden rather than themselves assume responsibility for active participation in a housing scheme and the obligation connected therewith. In this connection, of course, we have the experience of the housing scheme of 1919 and everything connected with it. With one or two outstanding exceptions, such as the city of Winnipeg, the municipal administration of the 1919 housing effort is not something to which we can point with very much pride. However, either method is available to the municipality concerned.
One of the most important reasons, to which I referred briefly a moment or two ago, for making provision for loans at low rates of interest to limited dividend corporations, of course is that they can initiate their programs immediately, in most cases I believe without waiting for the action of provincial legislatures or governments authorizing the guarantee of loans made by the dominion. I suppose some hon. members will be surprised to learn that in at least one of our great cities-in fact I know it is the case in more than one, but in one particularly-the work has been very much advanced along this line. A great deal of preparatory work in planning a low rental housing project has been done already, and I believe the group to whom I am referring will be in a position to get this work under way very promptly: It should be noted also that the limited dividend housing corporation has been tried 51952-2321
with conspicuous success in many instances in the United States, in Great Britain and in some other of the northern European countries. Many such corporations have had quite remarkable records, even during the depression. Those who have invested their capital have found not a lucrative but at least a fairly satisfactory investment for their personal funds, and I am hoping that as a result of the present program we may be able to induce leading business men in many communities to devote their time, ingenuity and experience to the organization and management of limited dividend housing corporations. While their monetary dividends will be small I think the dividends they will receive in personal satisfaction through having made a contribution to the solution of the housing problem ought to be ample compensation.

For the sake of illustration I think I am at liberty to draw on some of .the results worked out in one of our largest cities, where building costs are high but where a great deal of time and ingenuity have been devoted to working out detailed plans for what was intended to be a low rental housing project to be built and managed by a limited: dividend corporation. The group of responsible business men behind this scheme I think deserve the commendation of Canadians generally for getting down to hard work on a specific project rather

speechtext:
It is seven-eighths per cent half yearly for interest and one per cent for amortization; twice If per cent is 3f per cent. A five per cent dividend on the twenty per cent equity would be $10,800. Municipal taxes at one per cent of the cost of construction would be $10,800. The cost of management expenses, heating, maintenance and repairs, allowance for vacancies, et cetera, has been checked carefully by many interested parties, and is put at $32,000. The total annual carrying charge on the project would be $86,000, which includes a five per cent dividend on the twenty per cent equity

This means an annual carrying charge per average dwelling of $215. The rental per month of a heated apartment would be just under $18. It must be remembered that this is an apartment project and that these rentals cover heating. For an unheated apartment the rental would be between $15 and $16 per month. Of course smaller units could be rented for a proportionately smaller amount. I give this merely for illustration purposes and as evidence of the work that is being done along these lines in some of our larger communities. In other communities where the average family unit could be constructed at a lower figure, proportionately lower rentals would be possible. If still lower rents are desired than are provided for by an estimate such as this, they could be secured by the municipality or the provincial government or both making voluntary contributions to a rent reduction fund. In other words, this program makes it possible for municipalities to attain any results they wish in the way of rent if they are prepared to make the appropriate contributions.
The third part of this bill is unique. It is designed for the purpose of making a direct attack over the next three years on what is believed by many to be the major factor retarding house construction in this country. I may say that the idea back of part III was communicated to me particularly by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) in connection with a small scale experiment which has been made in the town of Burlington, and by other members who have not been following it quite as closely but who have called my attention to what has been made possible through a combination of the old Dominion Housing Act with the principle now laid down in part III of the bill now before the house.
While there are other factors, I think most will admit that the cost of real property taxes in our municipalities is the most important deterrent to the construction of new homes. In many municipalities the taxes are so high that many people prefer to live in a rented house and let the landlord worry about taxes and the carrying charges on his investment. If we ask why taxes are so high we find ourselves in a vicious circle. To an important degree taxes are high because relief costs are high. Relief costs are high because unemployment exists, and unemployment exists because, among other things, there is little construction work being carried on. It follows, therefore, that if we can stimulate the construction industry we will create employment. The creating of employment will decrease the

National Housing Act
burden of relief charges upon our municipalities and thus tend to lessen, other things being equal, the burden of taxes upon existing real estate.
It is therefore proposed in part III of the bill now under consideration that the Minister of Finance, with the approval of the governor hi council, shall be authorized to pay the municipal taxes levied upon a house, the construction of which begins between June 1, 1938, and December 31, 1940, up to the following amounts:
100 per cent of such taxes for the first year in which the house is taxed;
50 per cent of such taxes for the second year in which the house is taxed; and
25 per cent of such taxes for the third year in which the house is taxed.
Municipal taxes are defined to include the general municipal tax and the school tax, but excluding special and local improvement taxes. The minister pays only the increase in such taxes due to the construction of the new house. The principal conditions to be complied with are relatively simple. As an evidence of good faith, having regard to the dominion's contribution under this part III, we think that municipalities owning considerable numbers of lots suitable for the building of low cost homes should cooperate by making such lots available at a figure not to exceed $50 each to people who want to build low cost homes. Many of our municipalities are doing this already in various ways and we think it should be a condition of the dominion's grant in aid of municipal taxation.
The second condition is that the cost of the construction of the house must not exceed $4,000. Municipal taxation assistance is confined entirely to low cost homes. I should have said in connection with the first condition regarding the municipality making land available that this does not mean that the assistance by way of grants from the dominion is confined to low cost homes built upon lands supplied by the municipalities. The assistance in connection with municipal taxation is intended to apply to the increased municipal taxation brought about by the construction of any home anywhere in Canada which costs under $4,000 to erect. The house must be built by a person for his own occupation and the owner of the house must be released by the municipality from paying any part of the taxes which the dominion pays. Naturally, this taxation subsidy is not given with respect to any house constructed under part II of the bill which deals with low rental housing, but it would apply to houses constructed under part I.
If we can by this means stimulate the construction of new houses which would otherwise not be built, we will have done a great deal to reduce the costs of unemployment and the consequent burdens upon our municipalities. Apart from the vitally important social advantages of restoring the employable unemployed to normal employment again, existing property owners should benefit in a direct financial sense by the consequent reduction in tax burdens for the relief of the unemployed and by the fact that there are being created a larger number of units to carry the burden of taxation. Of course, it is impossible to predict how many houses will be built prior to December 31, 1940, as a result of the stimulus given by this part of the new bill. However, if we assume that the houses eligible for this tax subsidy are constructed during the three years to the value of $100,000,000, we can make certain estimates as to the volume of employment created and .the aggregate cost to the dominion.
We assume that as a result of this volume of construction municipal assessments will be increased by the same amount, namely, $100,000.000, and that the average tax rate is two and a half per cent of the cost. When we bear in mind that assessments of improvements are frequently on the basis of 60 to 75 per cent, or less, I think these assumptions are reasonably safe. In that case the total cost to the dominion would be less than $5,000,000 for the three-year period.
It has frequently been estimated that eighty per cent of every dollar spent in house building goes to labour, either direct or indirect. If this estimate be correct, the $100,000,000 spent on the construction of low cost housing during the next three years would provide $80,000,000 in wages to workmen in the construction trades and in the building material and supply industries, and the result would be, if that were true, that for every $1,000 paid in wages the tax subsidy would cost the dominion about $54.70-and that is very much cheaper than relief.
Some members, of course, will regard these figures as extremely optimistic, and prefer to make their own calculations. However, even after making a considerable allowance for a margin of error, I think the house will still agree that if employment can be created by this method it will be amply worth while to the Dominion of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, studying as I have studied during the last three years this housing problem and the manner in which it has been met in various countries, I reached the
National Housing Act

conclusion long ago that we would of necessity have to evolve in Canada a plan suitable for Canadian conditions. There is scarcely a country in which an attack has been made on this problem which has not experimented over a long period of years with different types of legislation before finding the best means of dealing with the problem. Indeed, in many countries which are most progressive in this regard there are several different types of schemes in operation. We have had the advantage up to date of our experience only under the Dominion Housing Act, supplemented during the last year with our experience under the Home Improvement Act. We believe that with the best will in the world this parliament cannot make a success of any housing scheme without a broad degree of cooperation from many sections of the Canadian public.
In the first place, to my mind it is most important to rid the mind of the man of small means of the fear which is there now of the responsibility involved in building even a low cost home for himself. Fear is very largely the cause of this depression, and on this continent particularly it is a fear which has not the same justification as it has in Europe. In Europe, close to all of the international difficulties now existing, people fear war. We may fear it on this continent, but at least, Mr. Speaker, the centre of disturbance is five thousand miles away from us. Our fears on this continent rest upon a different basis, and they have been existing now for several years.
The evidences of fear on the part of people of small means who have small savings are found in the growing savings deposits in our banks and trust companies. People in many cases would rather put their money into the safe keeping of institutions which they deem to be safe than attain the ambition of a lifetime by the ownership of a home of their own, involving a commitment for the future, rendered uncertain in their view because of the high taxation, the uncertainty of employment, and this widespread fear of depression.
If the government and parliament of this country can, by the degree of cooperation involved in the three parts of this act, stimulate the man of small means through the knowledge that his parliament and his government have faith in the future of the country, and that the people as a whole are willing to put their credit behind the small man, and are willing to give to him advantages-ease of payments, ease of cost, contributing towards his load of taxation-something worth while will have been accomplished.

I know what it means when a man is contemplating building a small home. The big costs come in the first year; a thousand and one things happen to increase his burden of expenditure during that period. I know what it will mean to thousands of artisans in this country to know that for the first year there will be no tax bill with respect to municipal and school taxes on that house; that for the second year there will be only fifty per cent, and for the third year only seventy-five per cent. I know what it will mean to people of small means to come within the provisions of the low cost housing features of this bill.
One of the great objectives, therefore, is to cooperate to cast out fear on the part of those who must initiate this scheme through their desire to own a home of their own, which is one of the most healthy aspirations in the breast of any man.
Secondly, and this is vitally important, we must have the hearty cooperation of those great trustee institutions of the savings of the people of Canada in the form of life insurance companies. The people of Canada have displayed their faith in life insurance to a degree that is exceeded by only one other nation on the face of the earth, and the sums entrusted to our life insurance organizations are immense. The responsibility for their investment is very great, and I know that those responsible for the investment of such funds feel their responsibility very keenly. I do say that this legislation is designed to cast out fear on the part of those investment institutions also, and to encourage them, as partners with the parliament of Canada, to make advances for the purpose of building homes not merely in our larger great centres where everything is easy, and where salability of property in case of foreclosure is relatively greater, but also in the smaller centres throughout the country. The tendency in the 1 st few years with respect to the financing of homes has been to accelerate the growth of our great communities and to retard the normal growth of those small communities throughout Canada which are still the backbone of our country. We must therefore get the cooperation of the lending institutions. They have a great stake, and I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that they will see their way clear to cooperate one hundred per cent in the carrying out of the objectives of this bill.
Then we also require in connection with certain parts of the bill the cooperation, of course, of the municipalities, in the setting up of the local housing authorities, providing for adequate zoning and planning ordinances, granting the partial tax exemption called for

National Housing Act
under part II of the bill relating to low rental housing, and doing real constructive work on the planning of low rental housing objects.
We desire the cooperation of the provincial governments in providing legislation, where legislation is necessary, because of the character of their existing laws; in giving leadership, we hope, and direction to the municipalities within the province, and in giving the provincial guarantee where low rental projects must be carried on by a local housing authority which is municipal in character.
Last, but not least, the construction industry. I hope that none of my friends, members of parliament who may have connections direct or indirect with the building construction industry, will misunderstand when I say that this legislation is a challenge to the building construction industry of this country, and is so intended. It is often stated that of all our industries, the one most laggard in advancing, in taking advantage of possibilities of improved technique, of lowering costs, of the standardizing of commodities, is the building industry. I do not join in that criticism, but I do say that there is one way in which anything this parliament may do in connection with housing can be killed, and that is for the building construction industry, capital and labour, material suppliers and all the rest, to believe that they can, by reason of it, start a steady upward trend in the price of the commodities they have to sell, whether those commodities consist of capital, goods or labour. We require the maximum of cooperative effort from everybody concerned; also, and not least, from leading citizens in every community. In this connection we are doing as we did the other day in connection with municipal improvements; we are stepping into a field which hitherto has not been a field of the dominion parliament, a field which, according to the opinions held by very eminent gentlemen, we have no constitutional right to occupy, and which we can justify entering at all only as primarily an attack upon our great national problem of unemployment. We require, therefore, the cooperation not only of all members of the house, but of all citizens, in what I sincerely believe to be a constructive, long-range, national housing act.

It is gratifying to know that the matter to which I directed the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) the other day was at least foreshadowed by a speech made by a member of the administration in the province of Saskatchewan. It will be recalled that it was indicated that we were to have this measure; and the minister was not quite sure, but "surely there must be some mistake" that the minister had said it would be approximately fifty million dollars. My information on that point, however, was accurate, as indicated by the press reports. In that regard I took the trouble to look up what happened to the Secretary of State for India, who published a telegram in India that had been sent from India to London; on his own responsibility he sent it back to India without consulting the prime minister or the members of the government; it was printed there and telegraphed back to London from India,-much as the speech made the other evening in Saskatchewan as to the intentions of this parliament with respect to a low-cost housing program came by telegraph to Ottawa and other centres of the country and was published before this parliament had been made aware of the proposal. In that case Mr. Lloyd George dismissed Mr. Montagu. A report of the incident will be found in the Annual Register for 1922. These words are rather important:
In the middle of the month a political crisis of the first magnitude arose owing to the publication of a message addressed by the government of India to Mr. Montagu. The message stated that the government of India felt it to be their duty again to lay before his majesty's government the intensity of feeling in India regarding the necessity for a revision of the Sevres treaty.
Then follow some details, and the record proceeds:
The publication of such a message naturally caused a widespread sensation, more particularly when it became known that the publication had been sanctioned by Mr. Montagu without reference to his colleagues in the cabinet. Almost immediately following on the publication of this message came the announcement of Mr. Montagu's resignation. The resignation waB announced by Mr. Chamberlain in the House of Commons on March 9.
National Housing Act

The report in Hansard of what took place on the 9th of March is wholly beside the issue here. But Mr. Chamberlain took the opportunity to point out that the doctrine of cabinet solidarity was so important that it must be preserved, and that when the Secretary of State for India saw fit to send to India and permit publication through the press there of a message which had not been communicated to the prime minister or the government or to parliament, his resignation should be sought, as it was; and he ceased to occupy his position.
There is an issue here, as I think the Minister of Justice was quick to grasp the other day, an important principle. A very important proposal involving fifty millions of public money is made known to the people of Canada through a speech delivered by a member of the administration in the far-off province of Saskatchewan, which is then telegraphed to this city and to other cities of the dominion. Such, of course, is in contravention of the rules that govern in respect to matters of this kind. I only point out the Montagu case because it happens to be the most recent outstanding case where a departure from the rules governing cabinet solidarity brought about the enforced resignation of the minister who had offended.
The legislation which is to be based on the resolution must naturally be followed with great interest by every member of the house. I think it will be agreed that it will be almost impossible to follow the details of the legislation if you look at the terms of the resolution upon which the legislation is to be based; for the resolution is silent with respect to the details with which the minister has furnished us. For instance, there is no indication of the rate of interest. There are no indications of many other matters on which the success of the legislation depends.
I am not complaining as to that. I do not suggest that the minister should be asked to furnish in great detail in a resolution the particulars of his impending legislation; but certainly matters relating to rates of interest have hitherto been held to be matters that should properly be indicated in a resolution upon which legislation is predicated.
Those who were then members of this house and who recall the meetings of the special committee which dealt with the question in 1935, and the discussions in this chamber on the legislation introduced by the former minister of finance, Mr. Rhodes, will recall that on that occasion he pointed out with great clarity that this was after all by way of experiment, and the authorization of ten millions of dollars was intended to be 
the beginning of the experiment which has resulted, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, in a fair measure of success, some seventeen millions of dollars being invested in these enterprises. The principle upon which it was thought possible to undertake dominion participation in low cost housing was discussed by a committee of this house, and at length in this chamber. The minister a moment ago referred to our lack of experience in this country. I could not help recalling the words of Tennyson, that we are heirs of the ages. For the minister knows, as do those who are responsible for what has been said as well as what has been printed, that this legislation embodies in terms, with respect to one part of it, the experience of other countries in a similar field of activities. The minister nods his head affirmatively 'because he made a passing reference to the point in his admirable address. We have then the experience of other countries in dealing with this problem. We have in particular the experience of Scandinavian countries and we have had to a lesser extent the experience of the people of England who, by reason of their form of government, have confined themselves to a smaller number of methods than those which are contemplated by this legislation.
The legislation, Mr. Speaker, to be based upon this resolution contemplates our occupancy of three distinct fields of activity. With respect to one the dominion parliament has given its sanction to our thus occupying the field, and the experiments that have been made in the days that are past have been sufficient to warrant the view, as the minister has stated, that we should continue our efforts in that direction. After all, a year or two is a very short time in which to draw an inference or a conclusion from the operation of any statute, as has been found in practice. But to the extent to which, as the minister has pointed out, our experience warrants it, we certainly would be derelict in our duty if we did not continue the operations of the act of 1935. That act therefore, in its essential features, is to be maintained, but the amount of money to be made available is increased. Broadly, that is the position.

National Housing Act
He said that the liberalizing regulations of 1936 did something to widen the operation of the statute. Now, there was no amendment to the statute that warranted those regulations; they were within the ambit of the statute as passed in 1935; and the modification of the regulations came about by reason of the experience derived from the operation of the statute, which was the intention as expressed by the minister of finance of that day standing in the position which the present minister occupies.
The other phases of the legislation which are to be modified in the light of experience are changes that have been brought about in consequence of the knowledge which we now possess. I think the minister made that abundantly clear. But when you pass into the second field of our activities as indicated by the act, there you have indeed the application to Canada of principles that have been found useful and effective in other countries. But they have attained their end by different methods. For there are constitutional difficulties in this country as compared with other countries where there is but one legislature to be considered in dealing with these matters.
One must bear in mind, therefore, that there are certainly grave difficulties-if I followed the minister aright-that must be met. Unless the provinces are prepared, through the creatures they have created, namely, the municipalities, as well as by their own act, to take the necessary legislative action, part II will not become effective. I am leaving out for the moment the question whether or not the legislatures will be called together to deal with the matter, but there is one thing that is obvious to every hon. member and that is that no municipality, in the absence of specific legislation, can grant special rates of assessment.

Now, we cannot interfere in these matters ourselves. We have no power
National Housing Act

as a dominion to make these conditions except as conditions upon which the loan is made. The minister pointed out what those conditions were. Whether they will or will not is purely conjecture, about which I shall at the moment say nothing.

speechtext: That is solely with respect to low rental housing.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
There would be another
way, but that is a way of which the government does not think well, and about which I shall not enter into a controversy at the moment. The imposition of conditions precedent upon the borrower-I use. the term "borrower" as a generic term-by the lender is again a matter involving property and civil rights, with respect to which action of the legislature may impair the value of the arrangement made. It is not like banking and commerce, where we exercise ancillary powers, as we did in connection with invading the field about chattel mortgages (Tennant v. Union bank), but here it is not a question of being ancillary within the decision within a more recent case in the privy council in connection with radio receiving sets. This cannot be said in any sense to be ancillary to it. In other words we have no legislative power to start with. Not having legislative power we are seeking to occupy the field by the imposition of conditions in a contract which we make for the purpose of lending the money -a contract not with the province, and not with the municipality, but direct with the borrower himself. The minister said just now that it is the only door open to enable us to operate in this field. I would say there

is another method by which it could be done, but that method the government do not desire to follow; they have made it quite apparent that they do not, so we will leave it at that. It will be recalled that this question did arise in this parliament in the days of the assistance given to highways, and in the case of one other statute as well. It is not necessary -to traverse that ground this afternoon.
With respect to parts I and II, I think I can summarize the position in a few sentences. First, antecedent to the exercise of our power, which must be by way of imposition of conditions under a contract, we have no legislative jurisdiction in the premises. That is apparent. Second, in the exercise of the powers we shall have to insist upon conditions being observed which, after they are merged in a contract, will not ;be subject to our legislative control. The minister nods his acquiescence.

With respect to the third field which the minister proposes to occupy, I shall be very brief. I need hardly say that the question of the federal government assuming taxes in municipalities is nothing new. The minister said it was unique, but during the last ten or fifteen years I venture to say there has not been a month during which communications have not been received from municipalities asking that local improvement taxes on crown property be paid by the dominion and that the property be made subject to municipal taxation. For instance comer lots are frequently occupied by federal buildings, and such lots when in the possession of other owners are heavily taxed for local improvements- that is, sidewalks, sewers, and the like. I agree with the minister that it is an awkward thing to have to remember; yet we must remember it. That is why I have been so anxious that we should have a constitutional conference for the purpose of discussing the question of the amendment of our constitution. But I am not going to do more than reserve the right to discuss the details in the fullest possible way when the measure is before the house, and I shall content myself by merely saying that as to the general principle I should think there would be no conflict of opinion in any part of this house. But I must say that as the undertaking has been outlined here to-day I think our right to act is dependent upon too many conditions over which we have no control; and which, if acceded to by those with whom we deal contractually, are still subject to the very difficulties the minister quite properly pointed out, namely the question of the right of the legislatures or of their creatures legally authorized so to deal with the subject matter of the security as to render it practically valueless from our standpoint, having regard to the extent of our advance.
[Mr. Bennett.1

In my judgment they may be improved upon by this house, by timely suggestions that may be made when the bill is in committee. We adopt the broad principle by supporting the resolution. We reserve in full the right to determine how best we may be able to achieve that end, having regard to the constitutional limitations which exist. Certainly at the moment I am not disposed to give my approval to an acceptance of the methods indicated by the minister, as being sound either in practice or in theory, as applied to this particular type of case, although I recognize that the minister has adopted one of two methods. There are only two methods open, and the method adopted is the imposition of conditions upon the exercise of a power, which conditions are to be embodied in a contract between the individual and the state, which contract is still subject at least to the general law-making power alike of the province and the dominion. In that way we may create a situation of grave difficulty from the standpoint of the country itself and in the administration of the legislation.

Certainly; it is a matter of contract. That is a fair way to put it.
There is just one other thing I desire to say to the minister. I doubt if any wooden house would stand a thirty-five year amortization plan. I merely mention that because certainly it is a departure from the rule that is observed in other countries with respect to wooden houses. Other countries do not do much in the way of building wooden houses now. All these houses in. England were of brick. The joists were not steel; they were wood, but the houses themselves were brick. In that case the amortization was not as high as thirty-five years. In most of the continental countries, especially in the Scandinavian countries, the houses are of brick; the joists and girders are not of steel, but of wood. speechtext: I am dealing with part II. It seems to me that this is all that I can usefully say at this time. I should like to study the details of the bill which I consider to be of much more importance than the acceptance of the principle. In other words, there is no difficulty about the principle; but there may 'be tremendous difficulty, having regard to our constitutional limitations, in working out the details.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it would be extremely difficult for any one to discuss the proposals made this afternoon by the minister without having before him a copy of the bill. One can discuss the question only in a general way. May I say at the outset that I desire to commend the minister and the government for the step they have taken in this resolution. In 1935 a report submitted by a committee of this house proposed a comprehensive national scheme, but nothing was done at that particular time. At last we are coming to grips with this most important question. In many parts of Canada house construction has lagged. Housing accommodation is required in many of our large industrial and urban centres. I believe the legislation to be based upon this resolution will give a decided fillip, may I say, to the building industry of Canada. It will provide homes and create employment. In addition it provides a self-liquidating scheme which will prove of inestimable value to many people in the Dominion of Canada. Some of the details referred to by the minister will have to be gone into quite carefully. The minister referred to municipal taxation, but this question is so involved that I would prefer to see the bill before passing any judgment upon the point. The minister stated that the taxation could not exceed one per cent of the value of the house built.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

Under part II, one per
cent of the cost of the project.

In other words, if a house
costs $4,000-

Even so, the point I wish
to make is the same. I have always objected to the creating of a preferred class of citizen in any community, especially in connection with taxation. Under this plan we are creating a class which is to be given preferential treatment over other sections of the community.
National Housing Act

The minister has pointed out that under this scheme homes or apartments will be rented at from $15 to $18 a month. If those are suitable for accommodating small families, I believe that we shall be meeting the situation in a reasonable way.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

I hope my hon. friend
does not take my remarks this afternoon to be in any sense a guarantee. I gave an illustration which was based upon two years of work in one of our largest cities. speechtext: I feel the estimate given by the minister was a little low. subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: It would have to be on a large scale.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
About twenty years ago I saw certain plans which might fit into a scheme such as was suggested by the minister this afternoon. I do not agree with the stipulation as to the income of the family. I do not think the minister should hedge the scheme around with too many "ifs" and "buts." I do not think it is fair to stipulate that the accommodation to be made available at from $15 to $18 a month shall be 
available only to those earning up to $90 a month. The man who is earning $100 or $110 a month should not be debarred from the opportunity of renting a low-cost house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: He would be debarred only if there was some fellow earning as low as $90 a month who wanted it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: I do not think we should have even that stipulation. We should allow a little more discretion to the municipalities in choosing tenants. In my humble opinion the success of such a scheme depends upon the type of administration. As the minister pointed out probably the only municipality in Canada that was able to make a success of the housing scheme of 1919 was Winnipeg. I was a member of the council when the provisions of that act were put into operation. We borrowed money at 6 per cent and lent it to the borrowers at 7 per cent. With the difference in the interest rates that city has been able to make a slight profit on the undertaking all through the years. Many of the homes have been paid up. When we look back over the years it is almost inconceivable that certain municipalities got into the difficulties they did. My main purpose, however, in rising was to say that I am pleased indeed that the government has introduced this resolution, which is to be succeeded by a bill. I need hardly say that we will give it our wholehearted support.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had some experience with housing programs as head of a city, one in 1913. I opposed one in 1919. The city of Toronto negotiated with the federal government in 1919. A large sum of money was borrowed and many houses were built, but for the most part the scheme was a failure. The money was paid back by Toronto and the other municipalities. The result was that the general body of the taxpayers had to shoulder the deficit burden. In my humble opinion it would be far better if this government would give a certain portion of the income tax, say one-third, back to the municipalities by way of a subsidy, bonus or subvention and so aid building and construction. I think that would lead to more actual building of all kinds and construction than anything else. This bonus or subsidy to the municipalities should consist of thirty-three and a third per cent of the net federal income tax collected by the dominion and would help out real estate and bring lower taxes. In that way the municipality could prepare the way and build municipal institutions of all kinds looking to future requirements, as

National Housing Act
Italy has done. In the past four years Italy has been building various -municipal institutions with federal aid of all sorts to take care of municipal expansion for the next forty years in that country and so aid recovery and give work. But in Canada our municipalities have -been starved; they have h-ad no money for any public works. Go over any municipal public building and you will see old paint, old doors, and a dilapidated building. No new construction can be undertaken, and the result is that taxes on real estate are such that nobody wants -to own it. The average tax on property in a large city is a rent in itself, as every member knows, and through no blame to our municipal councils who get no aid and have their revenues taken from them.
I think the minister should do something about the mortgage and lending companies in Ontario. I live in the district of Eglinton, North Toronto, and at one time more than half the homes there, if necessary, could be taken- over by the mortgagee. They are not worth the price of the mortgage. If -the minister could rap on the doors of some of these large lending companies and force them to bring the interest rate down-6i -per cent is the prevailing rate in that locality where thousands of houses have been buil-t and most of the owners cannot pay their taxes-he would be doing something worth while, and get cheaper money for mortgages.
A housing committee was appointed by this house in 1935 and it did good work as far as it went, but the committee was somewhat handicapped. One good thing it did was to go to the Ontario government and ask them to give municipalities the power -to pass bylaws to allow renovations -to homes to be undertaken, on the grounds of public health and to stimulate building activity. Much good was done in Toronto. The municipalities were allowed to make loans for that purpose, and hundreds of properties were renovated without expense to -the federal government. But it would not have been so bard on the owners of the homes if renovations had been helped by a federal bonus, or subsidy as an aid to housing.
There should be some other form of subvention provided to assist the municipalities because people in the cities who are out of employment cannot possibly pay their taxes and are often out the rent, and it would be far better if the minister dealt directly with the larger municipalities and handed them back some of the money they have paid in income tax, and so aid municipal recovery and expansion and real estate.
As to the type of building, I have seen something of this class of construction, which no doubt will be built by local concerns under this bill, in the city of Cleveland, where large apartments have been built by the local authorities with federal aid. But one consideration, Mr. Speaker, is that the average workman will not move from the slums to another district. He wants to stay with his neighbour and the person from whom he gets his house supplies. That was brought out in the evidence before the 1 ousing committee in 1935 and was so in the case of Leeds, England. They want to deal with the same grocer and the same butcher and get credit, and so they hesitate to move to some new district where the local authorities are receiving governmental assistance in housing projects; they could not pay the rents anyway. The question of transportation also comes in for the suburban worker. It is one of the main factors in housing and slum clearance and all other factors depend on it.
I asked the government early in the life of this session if they were going to bring down any housing or slum clearing legislation, and the minister said no; there would be only the housing act and the home improvement plan legislation, and now at this late date this large sum of money is being provided.
I have read the text of the resolution, and in my opinion it will be a good thing for some people, and the loan companies, but the property owners are becoming very much scared of legislation of this kind. It is class legislation for the benefit of the big loan companies and other large institutions; that is all it is. If the minister wants to do something to help the building and construction industries, let him hand back one-third of the income tax to the large cities, as a bonus or subvention to industry, the income tax which they have paid. The cause of the suburban worker is also being forgotten, the man who owns his own little place. I fear the new deal will not be an improvement.
