speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it was with a good deal of satisfaction that those of us who have been particularly interested in this great national question of housing surveyed the resolution which is on the order paper to-day, and which has been so ably spoken to by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) this afternoon. I quite agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he said that there should be no objection in any part of the house to the purpose of the bill which is to be brought down by the minister.
The house will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was my privilege last session to introduce a
National Housing Act

resolution urging upon the government the necessity of considering this vital question in a practical and direct way, and accordingly it is with a good deal of personal satisfaction to-day that I have listened to the remarks of the minister. There are, however, one or two points that I should like to discuss at this stage and present to the minister for his consideration prior to the bringing down of the bill. I do not intend in any way, shape or form to discuss now the details of the bill because, despite the clarity with which the minister this afternoon has presented its purpose and principles, it is indeed a complex subject which cannot readily be grasped in the course of one hour, even though it has been so clearly presented.
But one point which I think is of extreme importance is the method of application of the moneys available to the municipalities on the basis of population. If one city has five thousand of a population and another city has five thousand of a population, in the one municipality, as a result of conditions in the last few. years particularly, housing may be a serious problem, while in the other municipality of the same size, so far as population is concerned, housing may present no problem. There could be no more money granted in the one case than in the other, which seems to me to be inconsistent with the situation that may readily exist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: The criterion in this bill is the urban population of Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Yes, and I am speaking of a city. It may be a city of fifteen thousand people, any city the minister may conceive of, with a housing situation which is acute as a result of certain local conditions in that urban area, whereas in another city in another part of the province or in another part of the dominion, as a result of conditions prevailing there, there may be no housing shortage at all. Yet the first municipality, in which there is a housing shortage, and which needs more money than the second municipality, in which there is no housing shortage, can get no more money than the second, and that seems to me to be inconsistent with the situation which may readily exist. In other words, there should be some terms in the bill relative to the need of the municipality besides the consideration of population only, which is a cold-blooded-on-paper fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me just a word of clarification, I doubt very much whether a large enough scale low rental housing project under part II would be possible by a small municipality, for the

reason that the costs incident to a small scale project would render it prohibitive for the purpose which part II seeks to serve.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
I agree; but I was thinking particularly-and the minister will appreciate this, I am sure-of a municipality where, say, some new industry had moved in, and as a result there has been a sudden demand for housing, with no houses available in answer to that demand. The result is that you have a population inadequately housed even though the municipality may be small. There are such places in Canada where perhaps a mill, or whatever it may be, has been built, bringing in new workers and causing a demand for houses. I was going to suggest to the minister that he give consideration to that contingency arising and insert in the bill such sections as will deal with that particular point.
In the second place, the minister will be aware, from his knowledge of what has been done in other countries, that in Sweden particularly, and in the United Kingdom as well, large tracts of land in the suburban areas of municipalities have been purchased by the municipalities for the purpose of purchase by individuals for the erection of small homes. If this is to be done by municipalities under this legislation, the taxes from these newly purchased areas are found money to the municipality. True, the lands have been purchased; money has been laid out to purchase the land; but taxes on that land have not been received by the municipality at any time because it has not been within the boundaries of the city. According to the minister's statement, as I understand it, the portion of the taxes that is accruing as a result of the improvements to that land is to be paid by the government 100 per cent the first year, 50 per cent the second year, and 25 per cent the third year. Am I correct in that? On the other hand, these are new taxes accruing to the municipality. In the case of Sweden and, I believe, in the United Kingdom, although I cannot speak with authority there, these taxes have been absorbed by the municipality as not having existed before. Perhaps it might be possible in drafting this measure to bear that fact in mind; for it has been of tremendous benefit to the new home owner in a suburban area.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: That is, that the municipality would absorb what the dominion did not absorb?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Exactly. In other words, the municipality carried its own burden.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
That is worth thinking of.

National Housing Act

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Yes; I think that is a point the minister might bear in mind.
The next point is that a tremendous advantage has been given the small home owner in the way of price as the result of standardization of plans. One does not like to think of a row of houses, each one exactly the same as the one on either side of it. On the other hand, various plans have been presented by architects in countries such as the United Kingdom, Sweden and Denmark where the house is a standard house in the main as far as its construction is concerned, although there have been various changes here and there which have altered the outside appearance of the house so that it gives the impression to one who passes it of being a house different from the one next to it, although actually they may be the same. They have gone probably to greater lengths in that regard in Sweden, where they have three distinct types of house for various sizes of family. Further, in the development of their suburban areas they have made provision so that the houses are not located on the properties in exactly a straight line. In some instances the houses are staggered slightly; in other instances they are set forward or backward, as the case may be. But that is beside the point.
It would seem to me desirable, in view of the fact that this legislation emanates from the federal government, that some thought should be given to the question of obtaining designs for small low-cost standard houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: We have that now.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: I know we have that now, but not down to 82,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: As low as 82,500?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Yes. The last competition was specifically for that class, and produced quite remarkable results. My hon. friend will have to pay for it, I am afraid, but he can get a set of the designs.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: They are copyrighted.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: I have seen the designs. But I understood there was some question whether or not the houses could be built in all parts of this country for the figures estimated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
That, of course, will
always be a debatable question.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
A $2,500 house in Halifax may not be a $2,500 house in Vancouver. The aim was to have a $2,500 house. I fully understand that. But I was thinking more
of the pre-fabricated or partly pre-fabricated houses, and it seemed to me that some thought might be given to that suggestion. It would have to be worked directly in connection with the municipalities where the houses are to be built. In the case of Sweden, where so much pre-fabrication is done, the houses are built of wood, whereas in England the same cannot be done, because the houses are built of brick. It might be worth considering that the government should work directly with the manufacturers or the mills in the matter of production of, for example, casements, frames and so on, which can be built to standard specifications. All these things tend to reduce the cost of houses.
I listened carefully to the minister's remarks, but I failed to hear anything with reference to any consideration to be given to the man who wished to assist in the building of his own home. There is a feature which, as the minister well knows, has been a most attractive one in Sweden, that if a man provides labour in the building of his own home, all that goes towards reducing his obligation, pro-rated, if you will-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: It is possible.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: -and because he supplies $200 worth of labour, the amortization is just that much less as far as he is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: It is possible, under part I.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
It is possible under part I? Again, I am not criticizing; I was just suggesting this, not having seen the bill. I am very glad to hear what the minister says.
Lastly-for I do not wish to delay the house any longer-it seems to me to be unfortunate that we introduce a bill to deal with this great national question of housing and neglect the blot which is upon the escutcheon of this country, namely our slums; for I can find nothing in the minister's remarks this afternoon that dealt with this ghastly situation. The minister well knows that those who are at present compelled to live in the slum areas of our cities will not find it possible in any way, shape or form under this measure to build their own homes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Part II is designed

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: But these men have no money whatsoever. They cannot shoulder 10 per cent and build their own homes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: My hon. friend has completely misapprehended the scheme.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
I think not.

National Housing Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Part II does not involve any investment at all on the part of the individual. It is wholly a low rental housing proposition for just the precise class of people to whom my hon. friend has now referred.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Part II is intended specifically to take care of the problem to which he has referred.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: To attack the position of those who now live in slum areas, those who at present are on relief, those who have no incomes, those who have no jobs? They are to be permitted to go to these new areas with nothing at the back of them, and no prospects?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
The municipality can
go even that far if it wishes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: But this rests with the municipality entirely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: They can go even that far.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

If the only way to clear slums is to provide houses for people with no income at all to get them without paying anything for them, then I must confess I am stumped. I cannot face that one.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: I do* not think the minister is stumped by any manner of means; for if he looks to Sweden he will find an answer to that. That is exactly what has happened in Sweden. The municipality has built the houses. They found it cheaper to build the houses and move those who were in the slum areas to those houses than to attempt to maintain them where they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: Of course that is beyond the minister's control. I admit that. subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES

speechtext:
That is within the bill? I am glad to hear the minister make that comment.
I think we may congratulate the minister, not only upon his presentation of the scheme this afternoon but upon the fact that it has been brought down in the way in which it has been. I was greatly relieved to see the scheme in view of the fact that last year, as reported on page 748 of Hansard, during the course of the debate on housing the minister said:
From the time of confederation all measures with respect to the building of houses have been provincial laws or municipal bylaws passed under authority of provincial legislation. We might as well face that fact. Recently we have been put in our place by a very high authority with respect to our powers. Our powers with regard to matters of this kind are limited very largely to paying out the money of all the people of Canada for the benefit of some of the people of Canada, under conditions which are largely affected if not governed by provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: That is it. That is precisely the condition.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: It would seem to me, then, that that difficulty has been overcome.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Really, that is all we
can do.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: "That is all we can do," says the minister. One may hope then that this scheme will be accepted by the provinces; for if it is not accepted by the provinces, then the municipalities within those provinces which may not accept the plan will suffer as the result of the lack of action of the provincial legislatures. I wonder then, if when the bill is introduced the minister will be prepared to state what he considers to be, as a result of the contacts he has had with the various provinces, the chances of the provinces accepting the terms of this bill. In view of the fact that throughout the length and breadth of Canada this bill has been heralded, first in Saskatchewan, and now in this house, a tremendous amount of interest is being taken in it; the hopes of many people are being raised; and it would seem to me to be very unfortunate to raise the hopes of those who anticipate that day when they will be able to build and occupy their own home, only to have their hopes dashed by the action of some stubborn legislature in this dominion which fails to cooperate as we sincerely hope they all will.

the experience of the last three years' operation of the Dominion Housing Act it would seem that it is almost hopeless to look for any loans from the lending institutions, apparently because the returns to the insurance companies have not been sufficient to induce them to take part in this work. I was prepared to put up more than the twenty per cent equity and to comply with all the regulations. I had plans for the home and I approached several of the insurance companies as well as mortgage companies, but they would not give the cooperation they promised in connection with the Dominion Housing Act. I even went to the mayor of the city of Edmonton and called up several insurance companies, but with the same result. The city of Edmonton during the fall embarked upon a plan with money obtained, I believe, from the dominion government for unemployment relief. The plan was quite successful. They built several apartments and private homes, apparently to the satisfaction of those who were in charge of the project. Of course, as the minister pointed out, the city has a large number of vacant lots and these were utilized for the purpose. The only fly in the ointment is the increase in the price of materials that have been going into homes. The remarks of the minister in that respect are therefore opportune and I wish at this stage to commend the government. both the urban and the rural municipalities. The municipalities themselves can make good use of the money. I would ask the minister what the maximum amount of interest will be to the private individual who builds a home. Will the maximum be 1| or 2 per cent?

Hon. members of this house can do one service in connection with this act-I mentioned it once before when speaking of the old Dominion Housing Act. The parties who could render great service and who render the least are those local institutions, local to various parts of the country, which have direct and peculiarly personal connections with people of given localities, provinces in some oases and counties in others. They are the most difficult to get to cooperate in this matter. The great national institutions have given a good deal of effective cooperation-many of them, not all-but it is characteristic of the smaller localized institutions that, with the exception of the Caisse PopuLaire in Quebec and one or two others here and there throughout the dominion, in general there is a problem where local institutions which are most closely in touch with the local people will not come into our scheme.

I believe that is true. There is one matter that I think the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Elliott) has overlooked in the case he put to the minister. There is in Edmonton, for instance, a life insurance company which has substantial sums loaned on mortgages. Owing to recent legislation in Alberta the solvency of that company is threatened. Therefore insurance companies have now, I think, practically concluded that it is unsafe to make any further loans in Alberta. The minute legislation was passed which took from insurance companies two per cent of their mortgages, they having predicated their reserves-that is the measure of their ability to meet their responsibilities-on the expectation of life according to the mortality tables and on a three per cent rate on their investments, this had the effect of reducing their capital by two per cent. And the other provision does away with payment of interest. The result is that the companies which have to maintain a reserve will not put it into mortgages in Alberta. That is the real trouble.

speechtext: My hon. friend was speaking about difficulty he had in making application for a loan himself. speechtext: I rather think the minister said one per cent per annum.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: The minister referred a few minutes ago to the money being lent at 5 per cent. Is it 5 per cent to the borrower, or 5 per cent that the government are going to charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Five per cent to the
borrower, under part I.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
That is what the rate
now is.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: At what rate is the government going to give that money to the loan companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
mean, what is the dominion's share costing the loan company?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
No. The money is to be
lent to the borrower at 5 per cent. What rate is the government charging the loan companies that give this money to the borrower?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
We do not charge the
loan company anything. At present we make up 20 per cent of the total amount. Under the new part I we shall advance up to 25 per cent of the total amount lent; that is, the dominion will actually put that money in.
National Homing Act

The rate which has been used, up to date, with respect to the dominion's share, if my memory is right, has been 3| per cent or 3J per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
The profit, so to speak,
has been from one to 1J per cent.
Mr, DUNNING: Yes. I shall have all that information when the bill is in committee; but at the moment, speaking from memory, I think the dominion's proportion is calculated on the basis of a cost of 3J per cent.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: There is just one other point. In his statement to the house to-day the minister said the average amount of the mortgages was $4,000. That is the total amount loaned by the mortgage companies on the homes built?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: The average now is something over $4,000.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: I am sure the right hon. leader of the opposition did not wish to leave any false impression when he was speaking of the effect of the two per cent securities tax recently imposed in Alberta. I understood that was the tax to which he was referring.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: He certainly endeavoured to leave the impression that it had had a most injurious effect upon the credit of the province, and that it had made it impossible for the insurance companies to lend money in Alberta. I want to make that perfectly clear.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext: That is exactly the impression I understood the right hon. gentleman to wish to leave. I want to point out to the committee that the hon. member for Kindersley said definitely that last year, before that securities tax was imposed, he had attempted to borrow money and had been told by the various companies he approached that they had not been making loans in Alberta for the past seven years, at least such loans as he required, in connection with a home in Edmonton. I hope the right hon. gentleman will not object to my pointing out this fact in this connection.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES
speechtext:
I am obliged to the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I did not intend to imply that the application of the hon. member for Kindersley last summer was dealt with in the light of legislation passed this year; if my remarks were open to that construction,
I very much regret it. What I did desire to say was that the legislation, even prior to this year, had had a most injurious effect upon lending by loan and insurance companies. It is a matter of knowledge to me they have indicated that in view of the legislation which had been passed with respect to foreclosures, {Mr. Dunning.]
with respect to the acquisition of equities of redemption and the undesirability of owning property with the taxes, that prevailed, the directors had made up their minds that they would be derelict in their duty to their policyholders if they took the premiums and invested them in real estate mortgages in Alberta. That is the position.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 145, to assist the construction of houses.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
